Does your dean ask, or just assign?

Rate My Administrator scores the things faculty actually live with: extra work handed down without asking, whether it's paid, retaliation, shared governance and following the contract.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

"Unprofessional" may be the most flexible word in higher ed. Too often it means you disagreed in a meeting, asked about pay, or put a concern in writing.

If a standard isn't written down, it isn't a standard. It's a leash.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Posting safely: describe patterns, not one-off details only you would know. A specific meeting date or a program you alone teach can identify you at a small college.

The How it works page has a short guide and video.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/#how

Committee chair. Accreditation report. Program review. Curriculum rewrite.

"It's just part of the job," until you ask for release time.

Extra work without extra pay or time is a pay cut. Rate whether your administrators ask, or just assign:
https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Board trustees are on Rate My Administrator too, for every California community college district plus the UC Regents and CSU Trustees.

They vote on budgets, contracts and presidents. Faculty and staff can now say how that's going.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Shared governance means faculty help make the decision, not hear about it afterward.

"We informed the senate" is not consultation. "We gathered feedback" after it was decided is not governance.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Students and community members can rate administrators too. Had a run-in with a dean over a grade appeal or a complaint? Questions that don't apply can be marked N/A.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Part-time faculty teach a huge share of college classes, often with no job security and no say.

They're also the least able to complain about a bad dean without risking next semester's assignment. That's why reviews here are anonymous.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/

Retaliation rarely looks like retaliation. It looks like a schedule change, a lost section, a sudden "concern" about your tone, a committee you're no longer on.

Patterns are easier to see when people can compare notes.

https://ratemyadministrator.github.io/
